title: Il Barbiere di Siviglia
facts: The opera premiered in Rome on 20 February 1816 under a different title: Almaviva, o sia L’inutile precauzione.
The premiere was a disaster: the audience hissed and jeered throughout, and several on-stage accidents occurred.
Many in the first-night crowd were fans of Giovanni Paisiello, whose own Barber of Seville was popular. The second performance, however, was a success.
Rossini composed the score in just under three weeks.
The famous overture was recycled from two earlier Rossini operas, so it contains none of the Barber’s own tunes.
Mozart’s Marriage of Figaro, composed 30 years earlier, is based on the sequel play in Beaumarchais’s Figaro trilogy.
In 1825 the Barber became the first opera ever performed in Italian in New York. The 17-year-old future Maria Malibran was in the cast.
Rosina was written for a contralto. Critic Richard Osborne calls turning her into a soprano the most serious distortion of Rossini’s intentions.
Richard Osborne, New Grove Dictionary of Opera (via Wikipedia)
After Adelina Patti sang a very florid “Una voce poco fa”, Rossini reportedly asked: “Very nice, my dear, and who wrote the piece you have just performed?”
The Act II singing lesson often became “a show-stopping cabaret”: Nellie Melba accompanied herself on the piano, and Pauline Viardot inserted Alyabyev’s “Nightingale”.
The Barber is considered one of the greatest masterpieces of comedy in music, “the opera buffa of all ‘opere buffe’”.
Beaumarchais’s original play had a similar story: poorly received at first, then a favorite within a week.
